unharnessed.meaning: Keeps the frozen bananas, 50% power, the flame "about the size of a lighter's", potassium arcing, the light show, frozen veggies and soil, magnesium/iron/zinc, the USDA advice and the backdraft warning. "in the face" is colour hanging off the fireball.
unharnessed.sense: Terms fit: "bunged one in", "No dramas", "harmless as", "Have a squiz at these too". "other big lots of metals" strains for "high concentrations".
unharnessed.authenticity: Sounds like a real Aussie: "You can't peel the buggers when they're frozen", "The missus chucked some bananas in the freezer", "cop a nasty backdraft fireball".
unharnessed.register: Solid level 4 ("Strewth", "fair dinkum", "bonzer", "squiz") with swearing kept to dad level ("bloody hell", "buggers").
unharnessed.tone: The bemused question and the helpful, cautionary answer both come through; "don't you dare open the microwave door" keeps the warning firm.
unharnessed.flow: Reads well; "other big lots of metals like magnesium, iron and zinc can be the mineral to blame" is clunky.
unharnessed.essence: Unmistakably the Q&A: puzzled question, explanation, safety advice, links.

engine.meaning: The answer is kept almost verbatim, but the question adds things the original doesn't say: "my bloody wife" casts the wife as an annoyance, and "ya old bastard" insults an unnamed reader.
engine.sense: "You're all bloody good, it won't explode" misuses "you're all good" for "don't worry"; "my bloody wife" turns a neutral mention hostile; "ya old bastard" has nothing to attach to.
engine.authenticity: Stage-Australian bolt-ons: "Crikey", "ya old bastard", "mate?", "ay", stuck onto untouched text ("Microwaves react with metals, bouncing off and cause arcing").
engine.register: Swearing stays within dad level, but the Aussie is bunched into bolted-on tags while most of the answer is untranslated, well short of level 4.
engine.tone: The puzzled, friendly question turns rude ("ya old bastard") and the wife becomes a grievance; the safety warning is undercut by "Well, Opening the door".
engine.flow: Jarring joins: "Anyway, my bloody wife", "Well, Opening the door could create", "nonetheless, ay", and the original's broken "bouncing off and cause arcing" left as is.
engine.essence: Recognisably the original Q&A, but the questioner becomes abusive.

yarn.meaning: Every point survives, with colour that hangs off the original: "Banana's chock-full of the stuff", "the fresh air rushin' in can give you a backdraft", "Not the way you want to cook your brekkie."
yarn.sense: Terms fit their contexts: "dopey question", "No dramas, it won't blow up on ya", "make a dog's breakfast of the inside", "won't cook your microwave", "magnesium, iron, zinc and that".
yarn.authenticity: Sounds like a bloke telling it: "So I bung one in the microwave", "Microwaves don't get on with metals", "What the bloody hell's goin' on there?"
yarn.register: Level 4 throughout, swearing limited to "bloody" and "buggers".
yarn.tone: Bemused question, matter-of-fact explanation, firm safety warning ("don't open the microwave door"), with a light joke at the end that fits.
yarn.flow: Reads aloud naturally; the switch to narrative present ("the skinny end of the peel ... is on fire") works.
yarn.variety: Varied: "Crikey", "fair dinkum", "the missus", "chucked", "bung", "chock-full", "No dramas", "dog's breakfast", "and that", "brekkie".
yarn.essence: Unmistakably the original Q&A, retold as a yarn.
